reasoning: The organ is kibid (plural kbuud), and the food is kibde. The short vowels of the organ word vary between speakers, so I am only medium confident.
Loanword baaS has an emphatic S. Taa marbuta after س is e. il- stays il- before م.
The English 'heated up' is transitive, so it is the doubled form sakhkhan, not sikhin 'became hot'. Everyday Palestinian verb.
A borrowed political term, so ق stays q. ط is emphatic T. Taa marbuta after ي is e, giving -iyye. Palestinians use the word in conversation.
Form II verb tabbal 'he seasoned', with the ب doubled. The English past tense points to this verb and not to a noun.
ق in a'3ud is a glottal stop. The initial hamza of أقعد is a vowel seat and is not written. hoon has a long o. Natural Palestinian request.
biddi plus the first-person subjunctive of faDfaD 'to vent', with emphatic D. -lak is 'to you (m.)'. Standard Palestinian phrasing.
Taa marbuta after ر is a. Common word for an evening get-together or night out.
Taa marbuta after م is e. Palestinians use la7me for 'meat', and also la7m.
The computer loan verb sayyaf (from 'save') is written with ف and pronounced f. It is a verb, so not seef 'sword'. The same slang is used across the Levant, and 7afaZ is a formal alternative.
The spelling without alif is the colloquial form, with plural Sawaabi3. The exact first vowel is uncertain and some speakers say iSba3 or Sbaa3. It also covers 'toe' in context.
Literally 'may God give you health', said in reply to thanks or to someone who has worked. The -iik ending is the m. 'you' object. Everyday Palestinian.
A legal and MSA-borrowed term, so ق is kept as q. Some speakers say 'aanuun. Both vowels are long: aa and uu.
ط is emphatic T, and the final hamza is a glottal stop. Used in conversation, as in 'internet baTii''.
Palestinian past tense is zi3il (adjective za3laan), with the i-i vowel pattern. Means got upset or offended, and also angry.
A formal MSA connective, heard mainly in educated or news speech. il- assimilates to ن, and ظ is written TH. Everyday speech uses mahma kaan or mish muhimm.
Palestinian has long ee and long uu: leemuun, not laymuun.
Simple noun, pronounced shams. Feminine.
The glottal after the article is written: il-'urdun. No case endings.
ظ is written TH. Of MSA origin but genuinely used in conversation for 'great', for example 3aTHiim! as a reaction.
A loanword from 'veranda' and not a typical Ramallah word. Taa marbuta after د is e, but the vowels are uncertain. Palestinians usually say balkoon or shurfe for a balcony.
Levantine month name. Urban Palestinian usually has d for ذ in this native word (aadaar), though some speakers say aazaar.
il- assimilates to س. Taa marbuta after ن is e. illi is the relative pronoun, and faatat is the feminine past tense of 'to pass'.
ع is the reduced preposition 3ala, and the glottal after the article is written, as in il-'usbuu3. Common Palestinian for 'most likely'.
Literally 'his head got big', an idiom for becoming conceited. The suffix -o is the Palestinian 'his'. Not to be confused with kabbir raasak 'don't worry about it'.
